newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury panel - summary of views on budget.
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury panel - summary of views on budget.

text.p: Following is a summary of views from the British Treasury's panel of independent forecasters, who were surveyed by Reuters on Wendesday for comment on the 1997/98 budget.
TIM CONGDON, LOMBARD STREET RESEARCH
The Chancellor said almost nothing about the upturn in monetary growth from about five percent a year in the three and a half years to end 1994 to about 10 percent.

Ten percent is not consistent with 2.5 percent inflation in the long run. So the omission in this area, the failure to talk about this, is the most important part of the budget. What he has failed to say is more important than what he has said.
GAVYN DAVIES, GOLDMAN SACHS

The economy is showing signs of embarking on an intense consumer-led boom...The inflationary explosion of 1987-88 happened quite suddenly and some indicators suggest that there is a danger of the same happening again in 1997-98.

Overall, we doubt whether the genuine fiscal stance, on the basis of the structural budget balance (adjusted for asset sales), will tighten much, if at all, next year. Thus the Chancellor will not do very much via the fiscal stance to prevent the nightmare of 1987-88 recurring.
(The above comments were carried in a research document, in which Davies was co-author, published after the budget)

PATRICK MINFORD, LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY It obviously is a cautious budget and I think excessively so. But there was a strong consensus against doing anything more. Within those constraints, I think it's a constructive budget and makes some useful progress in reducing marginal tax rates.

The main threat to the Chancellor's strategy comes from the effects of overtight monetary policy which is putting upward pressure on sterling and threatens his 3.5 percent growth rate. In my view he should temporarily cut interest rates in order to pull sterling down and underpin the recovery.
BRIDGET ROSEWELL, BUSINESS STRATEGIES
For the Chancellor to say that this is a fiscal tightening was a little disingenuous. The risk is that he hasn't tightened enough, given the buoyancy of the consumer sector.
On the other hand, there are bits of the economy which are still not doing brilliantly, so as a balancing act it went in the right direction

The risk is that it won't be enough and that interest rate rises will have to take place sooner rather than later. My own view is that he can probably hold off until after the election, but at that point whoever is chancellor will probably need to raise interest rates by up to a point.
Now is not the time to expand the economy, and now is the time to get public finances sorted.
MARTIN WEALE, NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL RESEARCH

A cautious move would be to have another quarter point rise in the interest rate, but if the current level of the exchange rate is maintained or if the mark goes on weakneing, then it's perfectly possible that he will deliver the inflation target without any further increase in interest rates.
It wasn't nearly as restrictive as it should have been. Reliance on interest rates or an exchange rate to control inflation is probably not what the economy needs at the moment.
ROGER BOOTLE, HSBC GROUP
(Due to take over Minford's seat in 1997)

The budget was prudent but dull. It was mildly contractionary, if the measures announced to reduce tax avoidance work properly and if the tight figures for public spending are adhered to. It may not have been prudent enough, however, to prevent the Governor of the Bank of England from pressing for further interest rate rises.
Kate Barker of the Confederation of British Industry was not immediately available to take part in the survey.
